Rebuilding Stream Flow History Where Gauges Are Few

Source: vignettes/articles/flow-change-sparse-gauges.Rmd
flow-change-sparse-gauges.Rmd

Many streams that matter to salmon were gauged for only a few summers, or never. This article uses the R package wet (Irvine 2026c) to rebuild their summer flow history from nearby gauges, and asks how it has changed since 1951–1980, at four streams in northern British Columbia that chinook salmon use: Maxan Creek, with five full summers on record; Swift Creek and Naver Creek, with 14 and 18; and Gosnell Creek, never gauged. One method, fixed before any result, runs at each and is scored on gauges it was not given.

The answer. In the chinook salmon life history timing window for spawning, mean flow over 2016–2025 was lower than over 1951–1980 at all four streams, by 15% to 46% from nearby gauges’ departures; at Maxan, Naver and Gosnell creeks that route’s 90% range stays below no change. Borrowed, the window’s lowest seven-day flow fell at Maxan, Naver and Gosnell creeks, clearly only at Maxan, and held at Swift. In the migration window borrowed mean flow shows no clear change at any stream. Snow over every catchment peaked lower and melted earlier. Borrowed mean flow scores worse in the spawning window than in the migration window at all four under Bulkley windows.

Where are the four streams?

The four streams are in northern British Columbia, two in the Skeena system and two in the Fraser. Maxan Creek flows into the upper Bulkley River near Topley, south-east of Smithers, and Gosnell Creek into the Thautil River just above the Morice River, south-west of Houston. Naver Creek flows into the Fraser River near Hixon, south of Prince George, and Swift Creek into the McLennan River, a Fraser tributary, at Valemount. Each borrows from gauges in a same-sized box around it.

Maxan and Gosnell creeks in the Skeena system, with the gauges each borrows from. The inset locates the map in British Columbia.

Swift and Naver creeks in the Fraser system, with the gauges each borrows from. The inset locates the map in British Columbia.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s spawner surveys find chinook in Swift Creek in most years since 1970, with a major spawning site within five kilometres of its mouth in the provincial records, and in Naver Creek in most years since the mid-1980s. Gosnell Creek’s record is thinner: adults found in one survey, in 2001, and three provincial records.

What is a chinook salmon life history timing window?

A chinook salmon life history timing window, or window for short, is a stretch of the year when chinook use a stream for a part of their life cycle. In the upper Bulkley River, the early run of chinook passes Moricetown Canyon before about July 30, and chinook spawn in August and September (Gottesfeld and Rabnett 2007, 355). New Graph’s species-timing table sets the Bulkley’s windows from that report, used here at all four streams: adult migration from May 1 to August 1, and spawning from August 1 to September 15. A window’s flow in a year is its mean daily flow. At every stream, flow peaks inside the migration window, as snow melts, and in the spawning window falls under a third of its peak.

Each stream’s typical year (1981–2010), with the two chinook salmon life history timing windows shaded: wet’s published daily flow at the gauge, or at Gosnell Creek’s mouth.

Which years are compared?

Each stream’s last ten years, 2016–2025, are compared with 1951–1980, the three decades before global warming sped up (Hansen et al. 2012); ERA5-Land’s snow covers all of it. Measured Stream Flow Against Its 1981–2010 Normal instead measures this decade at two long-record gauges against 1981–2010, a period already holding part of the warming.

How has flow changed?

Two routes fill in the years a stream was not measured. A gauged stream’s missing year comes from one nearby gauge, through a fit between the two over their shared years. Any stream can also borrow nearby gauges’ departures from their own typical flow, year by year.

Each chinook salmon life history timing window’s mean flow, year by year, as a share of its 1981–2010 typical flow (log scale). Large orange points are measured summers; the grey line fills the other years from one nearby gauge, with the band its fitted relation predicts; the blue line is borrowed from nearby gauges’ year-to-year departures. A small point is a year with no neighbouring year on its line. Black lines are the borrowed route’s typical departure over 1951–1980 and 2016–2025.

The drop in the chinook salmon life history timing window for spawning is largest at Maxan and Naver creeks and smallest at Swift Creek, and filling in each gauged stream’s own record gives drops in the same direction (27%–57%), clear of no change only at Maxan. Borrowed, the spawning window’s lowest seven-day flow fell by 26% to 40% at Maxan, Naver and Gosnell creeks, again clear only at Maxan.

Change in each chinook salmon life history timing window’s mean flow (top) and its lowest seven-day flow (bottom), from 1951–1980 to 2016–2025 (to 2024 where 2025 is not yet approved), with its 90% range, by each route the legend names.

The Morice has windows of its own: chinook spawn there from the first week of September to the first week of October (Bustard and Schell 2002, 27), so its spawning window, September 1 to October 7, falls a month later than the Bulkley’s. Under it Gosnell Creek’s spawning-window drop is smaller, 23%, and its range reaches no change.

How well does the method score?

Held-out scores of each window’s mean flow, over the gauges in each stream’s box: the median over gauges, where 1 is perfect and 0 is no better than the average year. The filled-in column is the migration window’s; Gosnell Creek has no record of its own to fill in.
Stream Filled-in record Gauges tested Borrowed, migration Borrowed, spawning Gauges scored
Maxan Creek 0.50 21 0.63 0.49 31
Swift Creek 0.14 11 0.51 0.43 13
Naver Creek 0.63 17 0.60 0.42 24
Gosnell Creek 0.48 18 0.65 0.45 30

Both routes are scored by hiding a gauge’s own record and predicting it from its neighbours. A score of 0.5 was set as the method’s bar before any stream was run. The borrowed departures clear it in the chinook salmon life history timing window for migration in every box and, under the Bulkley’s windows, fall below it in the spawning window in every box, 0.42–0.49, so those ranges carry that weaker score. Borrowed, the lowest seven-day flow scores below the bar in 7 of 8 windows and boxes. Filling in a record scores poorly in the upper Fraser, with 11 long enough records to test it, so Swift Creek’s filled-in change is its less certain route.

Does snow explain it?

Snow itself changed: over 2016–2025, peak snow over each catchment held 6% to 9% less water than over 1951–1980, and half had melted 9 to 16 days earlier (ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021), summarised per year by cd (Irvine 2026a)).

Flow in the chinook salmon life history timing window for migration rises with peak snow: the borrowed departures at all four streams, with 90% ranges above zero and 41–51% of their spread explained, and measured flow at all 8 snow gauges near the streams (named in advance at Maxan Creek, elsewhere the nearest two with long records), 25–62%. In the spawning window peak snow explains at most 16% of the borrowed departures and 31% of measured flow; the melt date explains at most 23% of the borrowed departures but 64–66% of measured flow on the Nanika and Morice. ERA5-Land’s 0.1° cells are coarse here.

Where could it be wrong?

  • Gosnell Creek’s flow is never measured. Its departures are tested only at the gauges around it, and its typical flow is wet’s published flow for the stream. At 29 gauges in its box with ten or more baseline years, that published flow in the chinook salmon life history timing window for spawning runs a median 21% above measured, and about 60% or more above at a quarter of them.
  • The windows are the Bulkley’s at all four streams. Only the Morice has its own cited windows.
  • Each filled-in year rests on one neighbouring gauge, and the earliest years on whichever single gauge reaches back that far.

Software and citation

The flows in this article are from HYDAT release 20260717 (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2021). Gosnell Creek’s typical flow and the hydrographs are wet‘s published daily flow (build 0f4f8ca; for these four streams, routed flow from the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium (Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium, n.d.), placed on the Freshwater Atlas by New Graph’s fork of fwapg (Norris and Irvine 2026)). Snow is ERA5-Land’s (Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021), summarised per year by cd. Spawner surveys are Fisheries and Oceans Canada’s NuSEDS (Fisheries and Oceans Canada, n.d.), release of 1 June 2026; fish observations are the Province of British Columbia’s (MoE 2024). The streams, lakes and catchments are the Freshwater Atlas’s (FLNRORD 2021), held in PostgreSQL by fwapg (Norris 2024), and place names are BC Geographic Names’. How each stream was chosen, and how the method is run and scored, is set out in wet’s research notes.

The software, each cited:

  • wet (Irvine 2026c) reads the gauge records, fills in and borrows the window flows, and scores them.
  • cd (Irvine 2026a) summarises ERA5-Land’s snow per year.
  • ggplot2 (Wickham 2016), gq (Irvine 2026b) and sf (Pebesma and Bivand 2023) make the figures and maps; knitr (Xie 2026b) and bookdown (Xie 2026a) render the article, all in R (R Core Team 2025).

The data were bundled at wet commit 52facd0; this build ran on wet 0.4.32, cd 0.6.13, commit 86989e3, gq 0.16.1 and commit aa082d0. To cite wet:
